* *PHYS** **[N]****3****420** **[/N]** **Topics in Contemporary Physics**

* *[T1]**

# Course Description

| Topics of contemporary interest will be selected both from fundamental physics (e.g., black holes, pulsars) and from physics with important applications to technology (e.g., giant magnetoresistance, blue light-emitting diodes and laser). Each will be treated qualitatively and phenomenologically. The objectives are to introduce students to the frontiers of physics, and at the same time to develop skills in heuristic understanding and explanation. Students taking this course are expected to have knowledge at the level of the introductory calculus-based physics courses: PHYS1111, 1122, 2041. Grade Descriptors A : Demonstrate thorough mastery of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining all the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to apply the principles or subject matter to familiar and unfamiliar situations, in a manner that would surpass the normal expectation at this level and standards that may be required at higher levels of study or research. Has the ability to express the knowledge or synthesis of ideas in a clear and cogent manner. A- : Demonstrate substantial command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining almost all the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to state and apply the principles or subject matter to familiar and some unfamiliar situations, in a manner that is logical and comprehensive. Has the ability to express the knowledge or application with clarity and accuracy. B : Demonstrate general and sufficient command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining most of the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to state and apply the principles or subject matter accurately to most (but not necessarily all) familiar and standard situations, in a manner that is logical and persuasive. Has the ability to express the knowledge or application in a satisfactory and unambiguous way. C : Demonstrate general command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining some of the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to state and apply the principles or subject matter to most (but not necessarily all) familiar and standard situations, but with occasional errors and/or in a manner that is fragmented. Has the ability to express the separate pieces of knowledge in an unambiguous way. D : Demonstrate partial command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining some of the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to state and apply the principles or subject matter to some simple situations only. Has the ability to state the knowledge or application in simple terms. F : Demonstrate little or no evidence of command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining the course learning outcomes, OR failure to meet specified assessment requirements. |

* *PHYS** **[N]****4440****[/N]****[T]****Topics in Nanoscience and Technology**

# Course Description

| This course covers the theories and applications of materials with a length-scale of nanometers. The selected topics focus on phenomena spanning from nano-electronics to nano-photonics. Topics include: growth and fabrication of nano-size materials, applying quantum physics to semiconducting heterostructures and quantum dots, band theory and its application to photonic and plasmonic crystals, physics and applications of nano-photonics and plasmonics, and applications of perturbation theories to nano-electronics and nano-photonics. The contents may differ from year to year, depending on available expertise. Prerequisite: PHYS3021 or its equivalents, or permission of instructor. Grade Descriptors A : Demonstrate thorough mastery of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining all the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to apply the principles or subject matter to familiar and unfamiliar situations, in a manner that would surpass the normal expectation at this level and standards that may be required at higher levels of study or research. Has the ability to express the knowledge or synthesis of ideas in a clear and cogent manner. A- : Demonstrate substantial command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining almost all the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to state and apply the principles or subject matter to familiar and some unfamiliar situations, in a manner that is logical and comprehensive. Has the ability to express the knowledge or application with clarity and accuracy. B : Demonstrate general and sufficient command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining most of the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to state and apply the principles or subject matter accurately to most (but not necessarily all) familiar and standard situations, in a manner that is logical and persuasive. Has the ability to express the knowledge or application in a satisfactory and unambiguous way. C : Demonstrate general command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining some of the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to state and apply the principles or subject matter to most (but not necessarily all) familiar and standard situations, but with occasional errors and/or in a manner that is fragmented. Has the ability to express the separate pieces of knowledge in an unambiguous way. D : Demonstrate partial command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining some of the course learning outcomes. Demonstrate the ability to state and apply the principles or subject matter to some simple situations only. Has the ability to state the knowledge or application in simple terms. F : Demonstrate little or no evidence of command of principles and subject matter in the course required for attaining the course learning outcomes, OR failure to meet specified assessment requirements. |
| --- |

# Course Content

| | Topics | **Highlights of Fundamental Concepts** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. | Growth and fabrication of nano-size materials | Foundations of thin film growth techniques, clean room technologies and photolithography. |
| 2. | Applications of quantum physics in different potentials and its applications in semiconducting heterostructures and quantum dots | Review on basic concepts of quantum physics and results of different potential wells. Applications of quantum physics in resonant tunneling junction, two-dimensional electron gas, split gate technology, artificial atom, single electron transistor, etc. |
| 3. | Essential band theory of solids | Periodic potential and Bloch formalism |
| 4. | Nano-photonics and plasmonics | Review on basic electromagnetism. Basic concepts of plasmonics. Application of Bloch formalism to photonic and plasmonic crystals. Applications of nano-photonics and plasmonics. |
| 5. | Applications of time-independent and time-dependent perturbation theories to nano-materials | Basics of time-independent and time-dependent perturbation theories. Applications of perturbation theories in nano-electronics and nano-photonics. |

# Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

| 1. | state and describe the ways that nano-size materials can be fabricated |
| --- | --- |
| 2. | apply quantum physics to simple semiconductor structures |
| 3. | solve various potential well problems and apply the results to understand the physics behind various nano-scale device structures |
| 4. | apply mathematical skills (separation of variables, Airy and other special functions, use of power series in solving differential equations, etc) in solving potential well problems |
| 5. | describe and explain the band theory of solids, in particular the Bloch formalism |
| 6. | describe and explain the basics of nano-photonics and plasmonics |
| 7. | apply Bloch formalism to photonic and plasmonic crystals |
| 8. | apply first and second order time-independent perturbation theories to solve perturbed potential wells, degeneracy problem, etc. |
| 9. | apply time-dependent perturbation theory to electronic transitions, optical properties of solids, nano-electronics and nano-photonics |

courses.title: Optical Physics
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the basic principles and applications of various branches of modern optics physics. Topics covered include: geometrical optics, waves optics, polarization, Fourier optics, introduction to laser physics and nonlinear optics.
courses.enrollment_requirement: PHYS3041 or its equivalents, or permission of instructor.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Demonstrate knowledge about optical elements/devices and how to use them to build basic optical systems
2. Describe and explainthe wave nature of light through the propagation of light, light matter interactions, interference and diffraction
3. Demonstrate the understanding of lasers and interpret the meaning of coherence of light
4. Demonstrate knowledge of modern developments of optical physics and optical technologies
5. Appreciate important applications of optical physics
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Electromagnetic waves
Wave equations. Harmonic waves. Plane, cylindrical and spherical waves. Superposition of waves. Standing waves. Phase and group velocities. The propagation of light, Huygen’s and Fermat principles, reflection, refraction, light matter interaction

2. Geometrical optics
Lenses, mirrors, prisms, fiber optics, aberrations, introduction to ray tracing, optical systems

3. Polarization
Nature of polarization, birefringence, polarizers and retarders, applications of polarization

4. Interference
Examples of two-beam interference. Stokes relations. Multiple-beam interference. Theories and applications of optical interferometers. Resonators.

5. Diffraction
General concepts of diffraction. Examples of Fraunhofer and Fresnel diffraction. Diffraction grating and its applications.

6. Modern optics (Optional)
Coherence and Fourier optics, lasers, holography, introduction of nonlinear optics

7. Advanced topics (Optional)
Super-resolution optical microscopy, optical trapping, metamaterials
courses.feedback_evaluation:
1. Students are encouraged to provide feedback on the course materials, the teaching progress, and the teaching methods in class, and through questionnaires and email exchanges.
2. Express your views (or ask a student representative to help you convey the messages) in the staff-student consultation meeting held every year.
3. Post a message on the forum of the course website.
courses.required_readings:
1. Eugene Hecht, “Optics”, 5th edition, Addison-Wesley, 2017. (Ref no. in library: QC355.3 .H43 2017)
2. F. L. Pedrotti, “Introduction to Optics”, 3rd edition, Prentice Hall 2007. (Ref no. in library: QC355.3.P43 2007)
3. P. W. Milonni and J. H. Eberly, “Lasers”, Wiley, 1988. (Ref no. in library: QC688.M55)

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Photonics: Materials and Devices
courses.description: A broad survey of the materials used and the generation, transmission, modulation, detection and harvesting of light by various optoelectronic devices. Emphases are placed on the operational principles and applications of both devices and materials in communications, data processing, light emission, lasing, light control, photovoltaics and photodetection, as well as on related state-of-the-art scientific research.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MSc Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg;For students in BSc Physics
courses.learning_outcomes:
(1) To learn the working principles of dielectric waveguides and optical fibers and related materials.
(2) To acquire the basic knowledge of semiconductor physics that is related to pn junctions.
(3) To learn the working principle of light-emitting diodes and related semiconductor materials.
(4) To learn the working principle of laser diodes.
(5) To learn the working principle of photodetectors.
(6) To learn the working principle of solar cells and related materials.
(7) To acquire the basic knowledge about light polarization and modulation.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction
2. Wave Nature of Light
3. Dielectric Waveguides and Optical Fibers
4. Semiconductor Physics I
5. Semiconductor Physics II
6. pn Junction I
7. pn Junction II
8. Light-Emitting Diodes
9. Laser Diodes
10. Photodetectors
11. Photovoltaic Devices
12. Polarization and Modulation of Light
courses.recommended_readings:
1. S. O. Kasap, “Optoelectronics and Photonics: Principles and Practices”, Prentice Hall, Upper Saddle River, NJ 07458, TK8304.K37 2001.
2. D. A. Neamen, “Semiconductor Physics and Devices: Basic Principles”, 3rd ed., McGraw-Hill, Boston, MA, QC611.N39 2003.
3. B. E. A. Saleh, M. C. Teich, “Fundamentals of Photonics”, 2nd Edition, John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New Jersey, TA1520.S24 2007.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Instrumentation II
courses.description: Principles, instrumentation, experiments and data interpretation of spectroscopy, thermal analysis, microscopy and other instrumentation. Laboratory experiments for practice and illustration of the subject matter.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MSc Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To gain a general understanding of the development of modern instrumentations and know their significance to the society.
2. To make connections of the concepts acquired in other physics courses (e.g. thermal physics, quantum physics and solid state physics) to practical experiments.
3. To realize that one should know the working principles in order to gain deep understandings when performing research with these modern instruments.
4. To learn some commonly used experimental techniques and facilities in physics research, and have the knowledge of other instrumentations not discussed in details at the class.
5. To gain hands-on experience with available modern instruments in the department by carrying out some experiments, such as thermal analysis, atomic force microscopy, and optical microscopy.
6. To acquire experimental skills related to their research for further studies.
courses.course_syllabus:
Transducers and sensors: (~ 5 lectures)
Types of transducers and sensors. Figures of merit of transducers and sensors: Accuracy, repeatability, resolution, sensitivity, dynamic range.

Signal conditioning, propagation and conversion: (~ 4 lectures)
Amplification: gain, bandwidth, gain bandwidth product, impedance matching.
Analog-digital conversion and sampling: analog to digital, digital to analog, Nyquist theorem aliasing. Transmission media: types, bandwidth and noise restrictions.

Noise: (~ 4 lectures)
Sources of fundamental noise, thermal noise, shot noise, 1/f noise, signal to noise ratio, noise equivalent power and detectability. Environmental noise: sources and minimization, electrical pickup, electromagnetic interference and radio frequency interference, power-line-coupled noise, ground loops, shielding, grounding.

Signal Transmission: (~ 3 lectures)
Filtering and discriminating, averaging. Phase sensitive detection, multichannel averager, gated integrator.

Vacuum techniques: (~ 4 lectures)
Pumps: rotary, diffusion, turbomolecular, ion, cryo. Seals, flanges, feedthroughs, and valves.
Pressure gauges: thermoconductive, ion, Penning. Gas flow: controllers, flowmeters. Leak detection.

Instrumentation for Integrated-circuit fabrication: (~2 lectures)
Epitaxial growth, masking, etching, plasma etching.

Medical Instrumentation: (~2 lectures)
EEG, ECG, EMG, magnetic resonance imaging, tomography.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Topics in Theoretical Physics (Introduction to Particle Physics)
courses.description: An introductory survey of major ideas and important results in particle physics. Topics include symmetries groups and conservation laws, relativistic quantum mechanics, perturbation theory, quantum electrodynamics, quantum chromodynamics, weak interactions, the Standard Model, gauge symmetry, spontaneous symmetry breaking, Higgs mechanism, neutrino oscillations.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MSc Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To learn basic concepts in particle physics at the graduate level.
2. To acquire tools or techniques for calculating high energy processes.
3. To know about experiments from accelerators and astroparticle physics.
4. To interpret experimental results within or beyond the Standard Model.
5. To apply knowledge of core concepts in physics to more advanced topics in particle physics.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Basic Building Blocks of Nature, Elementary Particles and Forces
2. Symmetries, Groups and Conservation Laws, Noether’s Theorem
3. Discrete Symmetries (C, P, T), CP T Theorem
4. Fermi Golden Rule, Decay Width, Cross Section
5. Dirac Equation and its Solution, Antiparticles
6. Quantum Electrodynamics
7. Electron-Muon Scattering
8. Parton Model
9. Quantum Chromodynamics
10. Weak Interactions, Parity Violation and V − A Theory
11. Gauge Symmetries: Abelian and Non-Abelian
12. Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking, Higgs Mechanism
13. Neutrino Oscillations, PMNS Mixing Matrix
courses.required_readings: Lecture notes provided by the teacher.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Topics in Theoretical Physics (Advanced Computational Physics)
courses.description: This course is intended to provide a solid training in the advanced techniques of contemporary computational physics. Topics covered include: classical Monte Carlo method and applications, algorithms in matrix operations and ODE PDE solvers, many-body system optimizations, A brief introduction to Density Functional Theory, random systems, and selected topics of current interest in computational physics.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MSc Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To appreciate the connection between computation methods and physics research.
2. To realize that one should perform detailed calculations in order to gain deep understandings of underline physics for many fascinating observations.
3. To learn some commonly used computational techniques in physics research, and have the knowledge of other computational techniques not discussed in details at the class.
4. To carry out calculations of some basic quantities (such as ground state energy, magnetization and magnetic susceptibility, single-particle density) describing properties of typical physical systems.
5. To make connections to concepts acquired in other physics courses, e.g., thermal physics, quantum physics, mathematical physics, solid state physics, and statistical physics.
6. To perform calculations involving diagonalizing Hamiltonian matrix with the Fermi-Dirac statistics, and to relate results to manybody physical problems both non-interacting and interacting particles.
7. To perform non-perturbative calculations by using the advanced computational techniques, such Monte Carlo integration for classical systems.
8. To acquire mathematical skills related to integration and data analysis.
9. To acquire and appreciate the use of random number in physics research. To be able to write computer program to generate random numbers and
perform simulations.
10. To acquire the basic principles for further studies on computer simulation of many-body systems.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Random systems
2. Matrix operations
3. Solving ODE and PDE
4. Monte Carlo Simulations
5. Density functional theory
6. Other topics, such as machine learning. Parallel computing.
courses.required_readings: Lecture notes provided by the teacher.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Topics in the Frontiers of Physics
courses.description: Topics of contemporary interest will be selected both from fundamental physics and from physics with important applications to technology. The objective is to introduce students to the frontiers of physics. The level of presentation assumes basic understanding of undergraduate physics.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MSc Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg
courses.learning_outcomes: To develop an awareness of what is happening at the frontiers of research in physics.

2: Inflation

6: Structure Formation
7: Cosmological Neutrinos

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Topics in the Frontiers of Physics (General Relativity)
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the theory and applications of general relativity. Topics covered include: tensors, metric description of curved spaces, parallel transport and Riemannian geometry, Einstein gravitational field equations, the Schwarzschild solution and classical tests of general relativity, introduction to cosmology, cosmological models, inflation as well as some advanced topics.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To learn the theory of general relativity at the graduate level.
2. To acquire methods and to apply them to solve problems in relativity and astrophysics.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Principle of equivalence.
2. Description of curved space-time, parallel transport, covariant differentiation and Riemann tensor.
3. Einstein gravitational field equations, the Schwarzschild solution, black holes, gravitational waves.
4. Classical tests of general relativity.
5. Cosmology, cosmological models, inflation as well as some advanced topics.
courses.required_readings: Lecture notes provided by Course Coordinator.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Physics of Quantum Information and Quantum Computation
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the basic concepts and applications of quantum information and quantum computation. Topics covered include: key concepts of quantum mechanics, single qubit transformations, quantum circuits, quantum algorithms, quantum communication, and quantum information theory.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Physics; For students in MSc Physics; For students in MPhil-PhD Materials Sci & Erg;For students in BSc Physics
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To understand the mathematical description of quantum states and basic quantum operations.
2. To understand key principles and applications of quantum information and quantum computation.
3. To determine key requirements for quantum computers.
4. Discern potential performance gains of quantum vs. classical algorithms.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Formalism of quantum mechanics
2. Quantum circuits
3. Quantum algorithms
5. Physical realization of quantum computers
6. Quantum noise and operations
7. Quantum error correction
8. Quantum entanglement
courses.required_readings: Lecture notes provided by the teachers
